1: Chapter 1: A Visitor on a Rainy Night
In Peñaseca it had been raining for three days. In spring, Lucía Romero's older sister had left for Madrid, and since then Lucía had run the village's small pharmacy alone.
At nightfall, she closed the shutters, counted what she had earned that day, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had barely lain down when someone pounded on the door downstairs. A man's voice asked, "Is anyone there?"
In the doorway stood a young man soaked to the bone, his left arm wrapped in a cloth stained with blood. He said his name was Diego Lobo and that he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
"I need someone to treat me," Lobo said quietly. "I can pay. Will three thousand five hundred reals be enough?"
He took from his jacket a letter wrapped in waxed paper. "This letter must reach the monastery of San Blas before May eighteenth."
For Lucía, treating that wound was child's play, but the letter unsettled her.
Even so, she did not take his money and only said, "At dawn tomorrow I'll take him to the mountain."
2: At dawn they set out. Lucía carried a basket on her back with bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

Halfway up the slope they met old Tomás Gil, who was chopping firewood. He set down the axe and told them in a low voice that the previous afternoon three strangers had asked at the village entrance about an injured young man.
"Take the trail, Lucía," said Tomás Gil. "The main road isn't safe." Lucía thanked him.
The trail was narrow and slippery. Lucía went ahead, stepping firmly at every step. Lobo followed her in silence.
At noon the rain stopped, the fog slowly lifted, and in the distance the roof of the San Blas monastery appeared. At the door a nun, Sister Inés, waited to receive visitors.
Sister Inés took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. "The abbess has been waiting for this letter for 2 years."
Lobo said to Lucía, "I owe you my life." Lucía smiled: "Then next time you come, fix the roof of my pharmacy." Lobo stayed at the monastery.
At dusk, Lucía came down the mountain alone. When she reached home it was already night; she lit the lamp and sat for a long time behind the counter.
